I am here today to represent the views of my fellow Compass Kitchener members and offer
a collective endorsement for the resident panel as a welcome and a necessary addition
to the public engagement process here at the city.
I and other members of Compass Kitchener were privileged to observe the resident panel in
person, thereby giving us meaningful insight into the process.
The resident panel, in our view, is an outstanding example of a thoughtful and effective public engagement process.
We believe so for four reasons.
First, it genuinely represented the city at large.
Most citizen participant initiatives are overpopulated with members of the top socioeconomic group.
By contrast, the resident panel deliberately selected participants who collectively represented the full demographic and geographic profile of our great city.

This diversity led to rich discussion that illuminated a variety of meaningful perspectives for consideration, perspectives that collectively weaved together a complex yet compelling narrative of Kitchener.
Second, the resident panel made consensus building possible.
The process used an effective consensus tool to determine what the group of residents could
agree to rather than what they as individuals may have liked or wanted themselves.
This innovative approach forced participants to resolve differences respectfully as opposed
to fight them out.
In an age of incivility, the resident panel conducted itself with integrity, civility,
and virtue, a true sight to behold.
Third, the resident panel promoted social learning, an outcome often elusive to many
citizen engagement efforts.
Social learning refers to the process through which individuals acquire new knowledge through
their interactions with and observations of others.
The resident panel resulted in residents learning from city staff about the challenges and constraints
staff experience in forwarding certain policy initiatives, staff learning from residents
by uncovering new insights to understand problems and identify creative solutions, and residents
learning from each other, including those with whom they disagree, to better understand
the variety of positions that exist within their city and the potential implications
of certain directions.
Though not all ideas made the final draft, participants respected the process, those
involved and their perspectives.
Fourth, participation in the resident panel proved to make a difference, which made it
worthwhile to participants. While other municipalities oversee processes that primarily
serve a marketing purpose, where the participation process consists of city representatives guiding
citizens toward decisions an administrator has already made, the city of Kitchener utilized an
innovative model that produced usable, tangible insights. One of the most reassuring facets
of the process was taking input gained at the meetings back to city staff and then city staff
reporting back to participants on subsequent changes to the draft, thereby showing participants
what they contributed mattered. This step showed the resident panel was anything but tokenism.
All told then, Compass Kitchener believes the city of Kitchener demonstrated itself to be a model
of resident engagement. For these reasons, Compass Kitchener encourages the city to continue to
demonstrate its leadership by making this process permanent. Finally, we wish to publicly acknowledge
the outstanding work of Angie Fritz-Walters. She was instrumental in creating and maintaining a
sense of openness at the resident panel, welcoming people's input, and helping them arrive at
consensus. Frankly, the city would be wise to keep Ms. Fritz Walters involved in this process,
given that she was such an important reason for its success. Thank you.
